A remediation plan is only as useful as the boundary behind it.

Before discussing tools or policy changes, choose one way sensitive contract information enters the business and follow it. Who receives it? Which account opens it? Where is it stored? Which device, application, and outside service can touch it? Record what you know and mark assumptions for verification.

We at Cloud2e connect that discovery to CMMC preparation through scoping and gap assessment. The work maps where CUI lives, establishes the environment being evaluated, and creates a baseline for remediation and documentation. The intended benefit is focus: teams can direct effort toward the systems, people, and processes that are actually part of the preparation scope.

Start with one real information flow instead of an abstract diagram. If the business owner and technical team describe it differently, resolve that gap before building the remediation backlog.

posts.company:
Starting remediation before agreeing on scope can turn preparation into a collection of disconnected projects.

A better starting point is a defensible view of where CUI enters, moves, and is stored; which users and devices interact with it; and which services support that work. That boundary gives technical and business teams a shared basis for evaluating gaps.

Cloud2e’s CMMC preparation services include scoping and gap assessment, remediation engineering, enclave design, and SSP, POA&M, and policy documentation support. The sequence matters: define the environment, establish the baseline, prioritize the work, and keep the documentation aligned with the implementation.

For a practical first review, select one information flow and identify its owner, systems, access path, storage location, and external dependencies. Record unresolved questions rather than filling them with assumptions. Clear scope does not complete the preparation effort, but it gives every later decision a more useful foundation.
